item.text: I’ll compare insertion sort, merge sort, and quicksort, focusing on what “nearly sorted” means for their worst cases, then run `echo done`.

For nearly sorted data, **insertion sort often wins when disorder is small**. Standard merge sort offers a stronger general worst-case guarantee; quicksort’s behavior depends heavily on pivot selection.

1. **Define “nearly sorted.”** Let \(n\) be the number of elements and \(k\) the number of inversions—pairs in the wrong relative order. A sorted array has \(k=0\). This is more precise than counting misplaced elements: moving the smallest element to the end creates \(n-1\) inversions.

2. **Insertion sort: \(\Theta(n+k)\).** Each shift removes one inversion, so insertion sort performs exactly \(k\) shifts, plus linear scanning overhead.
   - If \(k=O(n)\), its running time is \(\Theta(n)\).
   - If \(k=\Theta(n^2)\), as with reverse-sorted distinct elements, it takes \(\Theta(n^2)\).
   - Thus, its quadratic unrestricted worst case does **not** apply when the input is guaranteed to have only \(O(n)\) inversions.

3. **Standard merge sort: \(\Theta(n\log n)\).** A conventional implementation splits recursively and always merges. Each recursion level processes \(\Theta(n)\) elements, with \(\Theta(\log n)\) levels.
   - Even fully sorted input takes \(\Theta(n\log n)\).
   - Its worst-case guarantee holds regardless of disorder.
   - Adaptive variants can exploit existing order; for example, skipping a merge when its two sorted halves already meet in order gives linear time on fully sorted input.

4. **Quicksort: potentially \(\Theta(n^2)\) even when perfectly sorted.** Consider distinct elements, choosing the last element as pivot.
   - On sorted input, every partition produces subproblems of sizes \(n-1\) and \(0\).
   - Partition work totals \((n-1)+(n-2)+\cdots+1=\Theta(n^2)\).
   - Random pivots give expected \(\Theta(n\log n)\) time for any fixed distinct-key input, but the worst possible pivot sequence still takes \(\Theta(n^2)\).

| Algorithm/version | Fully sorted input | Unrestricted worst case | Auxiliary space |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Insertion sort | \(\Theta(n)\) | \(\Theta(n^2)\) | \(O(1)\) |
| Standard array merge sort | \(\Theta(n\log n)\) | \(\Theta(n\log n)\) | \(O(n)\) |
| Last-pivot quicksort, ordinary recursion | \(\Theta(n^2)\) | \(\Theta(n^2)\) | \(O(n)\) worst-case stack |

Choose insertion sort when inversion count is reliably small. Choose merge sort when predictable worst-case performance matters and linear extra memory is acceptable.
